title: New York's Bodega Cats: Beloved, Illegal, and Now the Stars of a New Book
summary:
In the cramped aisles of New York City's bodegas, among the canned goods and cleaning supplies, you might spot a tabby curled up on a stack of newspapers. These feline fixtures are adored by locals, but they're also technically breaking the law. City health codes prohibit animals in food-serving businesses, yet thousands of cats serve as unofficial pest control, keeping rats at bay.

Dan Rimada, a devoted cat lover, founded Bodega Cats of New York in 2022 to document and advocate for these clandestine shopkeepers. This fall, a book by Epic Ink will feature 120 photographs of 60 cats across all five boroughs, captured by photographer Gulce Kilkis. From Oreo in Park Slope to Prince in SoHo, each cat's story reveals a spectrum of care—some are pampered royalty, others barely tolerated.

But Rimada's mission goes beyond photography. He's spearheaded two bills currently in committee. One would prevent city agencies from automatically treating a cat in a retail food store as a violation, instead requiring voluntary vaccination and spay/neuter programs. The other would legally permit cats in stores if they meet veterinary standards. 'We want to protect what makes New York City feel like home,' Rimada says. 'And that includes taking care of the cats that are a part of it.'

The book, slated for November, is both a celebration and a call to action. It highlights the complex reality for these animals while pushing for their official recognition. As Rimada's project gains traction, the hope is that these beloved bodega residents can finally come out of the shadows—legally.
why_it_matters: The debate over bodega cats forces a young person to think about how laws sometimes clash with everyday life and local traditions. It raises questions about whether rules can be flexible enough to protect public health while still preserving what makes a community unique, and how grassroots efforts can slowly change outdated policies.

background_read: Bodegas are a staple of New York City life, often family-owned corner stores that sell groceries, snacks, and everyday items. The Spanish word 'bodega' originally meant 'wine cellar' or 'warehouse,' but in NYC it has come to mean these small, independent shops that serve communities, especially in neighborhoods with large Latino populations. Throughout history, shop cats have been common worldwide because they protect food stocks from rodents. However, as food safety laws tightened in the 20th century, animals became forbidden inside most food stores. In New York, the health code classifies a cat in a store as a violation, even if the cat never touches any food. Dan Rimada, a cat enthusiast, started documenting these cats online to show their personalities and the important role they play, while also pushing for legal changes. The two bills he advocates for aim to balance public health with the cultural reality of bodega cats by requiring vaccinations and spay/neuter procedures, similar to programs for outdoor community cats.

perspectives.description: Bodega cats control rats without chemicals, and they create a cozy neighborhood feeling that attracts customers. Many store owners and residents see them as part of the city's identity, and the proposed bills would make this practice safe and official, protecting both the cats and the public.

Health inspectors and some customers worry that cat hair, dander, or litterbox smells could contaminate food, especially in cramped stores. There is also the risk that not all cats could be trained to stay away from food shelves, and vaccination requirements might be hard to enforce consistently across thousands of bodegas.

This situation is an example of a gray area where official rules don't match what people actually do. Many other cities have similar conflicts—for example, food trucks and street vendors often operate in legal limbo. The bodega cat issue reflects a broader pattern of how communities push back when laws feel detached from their daily realities.

If the bills pass, New York could become a model for other cities with shop cat traditions, showing how to integrate animal welfare, public health, and cultural preservation. In the future, technology like microchip registration or health-monitoring collars might even help track the well-being of working cats, making the system more transparent.
